comments.text: My dad really tried to protect my sister and I from what he saw in the fire service when we were little. I can tell you there is nothing more magical than being a little boy whose dad is a firefighter. I got to ride the engine in parades, he came to speak to my class, we hung out at the station often when he had a weekend shift. But once I was a teenager he started to reveal more about what he saw on the job. The first big one was when I had just turned 16 a classmate and friend of mine attempted suicide. He made it to the hospital and was on life support, and my dad sat me down day one and told it to me straight, that he had friends who were at the scene and that my classmate was very unlikely to survive. There was a lot of false hope still going around, but he knew that I needed the truth. He was correct and having that time to prepare did help with the grief.   He’s told me about some other cases now that I’m an adult and I couldn’t be prouder of the work he’s done.

Former FR/EMT here.. 

As much as you see for years, seeing someone literally die in front of you while you’re trying to get an IV never, ever leaves you. 

I’ll share shortly why I’m not a FR anymore: My county was volunteer but I got my FR and EMT certs, and I was on my way to class (college) and I was on call. Got a call on my radio about a vehicle accident 2 miles from my location. Remember, this is a small, volunteer department. So I bypass class, rush over, all I had in my truck was my first aid kit, some gloves. 

I arrive, just an officer or two on scene. A drunk semi driver had collided head on with a van, carrying a mother and a child. 

I had to verify and assist.. mother was DOA, but I still do CP until the FD got there. 

The baby.. was in half.. 

I’ve seen cadavers, I’ve dealt with dying or dead elderly, trauma wounds. That was the first and last time I ever dealt with a deceased child, an infant. 

I quit two days later. 

Just couldn’t handle it. Those who have risen above and deal with this every single day are the true heroes. 

I love all my brothers and sisters in the medical field. ❤

Edit: THANK YOU ALL for the love and prayers. It’s truly amazing to see everyone share their own experiences! God bless you all ❤

I was in the process of moving my elderly mom from where she lived to where I lived.  She had terminal cancer.  Everything was set and we checked into the Atlantis Hotel (Reno) for the night to catch an early morning flight.   We thought she had about 6 mos. to a year.  She went downhill that night and was unresponsive when I tried to wake her up so I called 911 and gave them details and stressed room number.  Then I called the front desk and let them know so they could be aware and direct them to the room.  They got angry with me over the phone because I didn’t call them first.   I ended up hanging up on them.   I propped open the room door (we were at the end of a hall so privacy was not an issue).   Firefighters arrive en masse - there were at least 4 and 3 hotel employees who kept trying to come into the room.   God bless those firefighters- they were amazing. Two immediately started assessing / treating my mom.  One basically shooed the hotel guys out and down the hall a ways.  The fourth one, after I had given them all the medical history, got right in my face and looked me dead in the eye and said, “What do you need?  Your mom is being taken care of, what can I do to help you?”  I wasn’t panicking or distraught, I basically shut down and keep it all together in an emergency and then fall apart after.  It was so shocking.   I wanted to ride with her because she was scared.  But I didn’t know what to do with our luggage and the hotel checkout and the rental car because they would not let me extend our reservation.  The hotel manager said they would not keep my luggage and he wanted me to actually checkout even though it was all paid for in advance.   He was a total ass.  One of the firefighters asked if I was okay with him driving my car to the hospital. The firefighter loaded my luggage and drove my car to the hospital so I could ride with her in the ambulance.  They were so incredibly kind.  I wish I could say the same for the hotel people - they were so cold and uncaring.

P.S. to all who have commented or read this later, I think the reason hotels seem to get pissed is that too many times people who need 911 call them first (as they should) but then never let the hotel desk know, so they are unprepared to direct the emergency responders accordingly.

Just as a PSA, ALWAYS call 911 first, but then ALWAYS call the front lobby as well so that everything can be expedited.  This is true in a hotel, or an office building.   If you are at work it’s always a good idea to have someone go down to meet them at the loading dock entrance and one at the front of the building (you never know where they will arrive).   Also keep someone stationed both at the service elevator and regular elevators on the floor so they know where to find the person quickly.

Here in The Netherlands we have a system of volunteer cardiac first responders. These are civilians who have had CPR training an voluntarily sign up to assist professional first responders in the case of (suspected) cardiac arrests. 

I am one of these people. 

I do talk to a lot of people about this and I always get the same question: can I do something wrong when attempting CPR? And my answer is always the same: Yes, there is one thing you can do wrong: that is do nothing. Calling an ambulance, opening the door, point the ambulance to the right address, etc. would all be better than doing nothing at all. You don't have to do chest compressions (allthough it would be preffered if you did) to help someone. Just call professional help immediatly.

comments.text: 39:20 Air purifiers don't suck air into the room, they circulate air that's already in the room. So, actually a great idea to turn them on, no downsides. In fact, on a similar subject, if you know there's a fire in your house, and you have central HVAC which you can either control from your phone or get to the thermostat without endangering yourself, turning the HVAC off is also not a bad idea. Fire needs oxygen, and HVAC will keep pushing fresh air into any enclosed spaces. If the filter on the return air duct burns away, now it's potentially sending embers to other parts of the house and spreading the fire even more quickly.
